title: What is ethnography? Fieldwork, methods and examples
seo_title: What is Ethnography? Meaning, Methods and Examples
meta_description: What is ethnography? Learn its meaning, how participant observation and field notes work, the ethics of fieldwork, and classic and Indian examples.
summary: Ethnography is a research method, and the written account it produces, in which a researcher studies a group of people by living among them, taking part in daily life and recording what they see and hear. Its core is participant observation over months or years, supported by interviews, field notes and mapping.

sections.h2: Ethnography meaning: method and written account
paras: The word combines the Greek ethnos, people, and graphein, to write. Ethnography therefore means writing about a people, and it has two senses. It is a method of research, based on long and close contact with a community. It is also the product of that research: a book, article or film that describes and explains a way of life.

Ethnography is the signature method of social and cultural [anthropology](what-is-anthropology.html), though it is now also used in sociology, education, public health, design and business. It is different from ethnology, an older term for the comparative study of many cultures, usually from written sources. Ethnography goes deep into one setting. Ethnology compares across many.

sections.h2: Participant observation: the heart of the method
paras: Participant observation means taking part in everyday life while observing it carefully. The ethnographer joins in work, meals, markets, festivals and ordinary conversation, and pays attention to what people do as well as what they say. Over time, people stop performing for the visitor, and the researcher begins to understand the unwritten rules that everyone else takes for granted.

This takes time. Classic anthropological fieldwork usually lasts a year or more, long enough to see a full agricultural and ritual cycle. It also usually requires learning the local language. Shorter forms, sometimes called rapid or focused ethnography, are used in applied work, but they rely on the same habits of attention.
Alongside participant observation, ethnographers use a set of practical tools. None of them is complicated on its own. The skill lies in using them patiently and honestly.
list: Field notes: detailed daily notes, written as soon as possible after events, separating what was seen from what the researcher thinks it means.
Interviews: from informal chats to structured conversations, recorded only with permission.
Genealogies and kinship charts: who is related to whom, a classic tool for understanding households, inheritance and marriage.
Life histories and oral history: long accounts of one person's life, which show how wider changes are felt in individual lives.
Mapping and household surveys: who lives where, who owns what, and how space is used.
Photographs, audio and video: always with consent, and with thought about how images will be used later.

sections.h2: Classic and Indian examples of ethnography
paras: Bronisław Malinowski's study of the Trobriand Islanders, based on fieldwork between 1915 and 1918 and published as Argonauts of the Western Pacific in 1922, is often treated as the model of modern ethnography. E. E. Evans-Pritchard's work on the Nuer of Sudan and Margaret Mead's studies in Samoa and New Guinea are other well-known early examples, though all of them are now read critically as well as admired.

India has a long ethnographic tradition. Sarat Chandra Roy wrote detailed monographs on the Munda and Oraon of Jharkhand in the early 20th century. Verrier Elwin wrote about the Baiga, Gond and other communities of central India. M. N. Srinivas studied the Coorgs and later the village of Rampura in Karnataka. Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf worked among the Chenchu, the Gond and communities of the northeast. More recent ethnographies study call centres, courts, hospitals and city neighbourhoods, which shows that the method is not limited to villages or to [tribal communities](tribes-of-india.html).

Ethnography involves living closely with people, so ethics matter more than in almost any other method. Researchers must explain who they are and why they are there, ask for consent, protect people's privacy, and think about the risks their writing might create for the community. Many communities in India have been studied repeatedly, sometimes with little benefit to themselves, and are rightly cautious of researchers.

Modern ethnography also asks the researcher to be honest about their own position: their caste, gender, class, nationality and language shape what they are told and what they notice. Many ethnographers now share their findings with the community, return copies of photographs and recordings, and work with community members as co-researchers rather than only as informants.

You can practise the basic skills close to home. Spend a morning in a local market and write careful notes on who does what. Interview an older relative about how your neighbourhood has changed, with their permission and a recorder. Write up what surprised you. The habit of separating observation from interpretation is the most valuable first lesson.

Structured practice helps. The [oral history and neighbourhood memory lab](oral-history-and-neighbourhood-memory-lab.html) teaches interviewing, consent and recording in a real setting, and the [research methods and academic writing](research-methods-academic-writing.html) workshop helps students turn field notes into a clear written account. A visit to the [Bhopal Tribal Museum](bhopal-tribal-museum-material-culture-interpretation.html) is also useful: many of its displays draw on ethnographic knowledge and close work with artists from the communities shown, and it is a good place to discuss how ethnographic knowledge is presented to the public.

faq.q: What is ethnography in simple words?
faq.a: Ethnography is a way of studying people by spending a long time with them, taking part in their daily life and writing careful notes about what happens. The word also refers to the book or report that results. It aims to understand a way of life from the inside.

faq.q: What is the difference between ethnography and ethnology?
faq.a: Ethnography is the detailed study of one community or setting through fieldwork. Ethnology is the comparative study of many cultures, often using existing ethnographies and other sources. In simple terms, ethnography goes deep into one place and ethnology compares across places.

faq.q: How long does ethnographic fieldwork take?
faq.a: Classic anthropological fieldwork usually lasts at least a year, so that the researcher sees a full seasonal and ritual cycle and learns the local language. Applied projects sometimes use shorter, focused ethnography of a few weeks, but these depend on clear questions and earlier knowledge of the setting.

faq.q: Who is called the father of ethnography?
faq.a: Bronisław Malinowski is often called the father of modern ethnography because of his long fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands between 1915 and 1918 and his emphasis on participant observation. In India, Sarat Chandra Roy is remembered for pioneering ethnographic monographs on the Munda and Oraon.

Yes. Ethnography is one of the main forms of qualitative research, because it relies on observation, conversation and interpretation rather than numbers. Many ethnographers also collect some quantitative data, such as household surveys or land records, to support what they observe.

posts.hook: Ethnography means, quite literally, writing about people.
posts.caption: From the Greek ethnos and graphein, it is both a method and the book that results. Malinowski's Trobriand fieldwork set the model, and Sarat Chandra Roy pioneered it in India. Read our guide.

posts.hook: The first rule of field notes.
posts.caption: Write down what you saw before you write down what you think it means. Keep the two in separate columns. It sounds simple, and it changes everything about how you observe.
